drug_name: Desogestrel and Ethinyl Estradiol / Ethinyl Estradiol
what_its_for: This medicine is a combination birth control pill (oral contraceptive) used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two female hormones — a progestin (desogestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol). Some packs also include low-dose estrogen-only pills to help maintain hormone levels during the last week of the cycle.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day, at the same time each day, with or without food. It helps to pick a time that is easy to remember, such as bedtime or with a morning meal. Take the pills in the exact order shown on the pack — do not skip or rearrange them. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days when you start this medicine for the first time.
dosing: One tablet taken by mouth once daily for 28 days. Your pack contains active hormone pills (usually for 21 days), followed by reminder or low-dose estrogen pills (for 7 days). Start a new pack the day after you finish the last pill of your current pack — do not take a break between packs. Your period will typically come during the reminder pill days.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 active pill, take it as soon as you remember, even if it means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue taking 1 pill per day as usual — no backup birth control is needed. If you miss 2 active pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2, take 2 pills the day you remember and 2 pills the next day, then continue 1 pill daily. Use a backup method for 7 days. If you miss 2 or more active pills in Week 3, or miss 3 or more pills in a row at any time, throw out the rest of the pack and start a new pack the same day. Use backup birth control for 7 days. If you miss reminder or low-dose estrogen pills, just throw them away and continue the pack — your protection is not affected. If you miss pills and have had unprotected sex, consider emergency contraception and call your doctor.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired pills safely — do not flush down the toilet unless instructed to do so.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking, especially if you are over 35 years old — combining smoking with this pill greatly increases your risk of serious heart and blood vessel problems, including blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice in large amounts, as it may affect how the medicine works. Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, as some drugs (like rifampin, certain seizure medicines, St. John's Wort, and some HIV medicines) can make your birth control less effective. Avoid prolonged bed rest or long periods of sitting still (such as long flights), as these can increase the risk of blood clots while on this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of these warning signs — sometimes remembered as 'ACHES': Abdominal pain (severe); Chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood; Headaches that are severe or unusual; Eye problems such as blurred vision, flashing lights, or vision loss; Severe leg pain or swelling in the calf. Also contact your doctor if you have: signs of a blood clot (leg swelling, warmth, or redness); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); severe depression or mood changes; breast lumps; no period for two months in a row; or any unusual or concerning symptoms.
when_it_works: If you start this pill on the first day of your period, you are protected against pregnancy right away. If you start on any other day, use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days. It may take 1 to 3 months for your body to fully adjust to the hormones — you might have irregular spotting or light bleeding during this adjustment period. This is normal.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking this pill, stop taking it and contact your doctor. Breastfeeding: This medicine is generally not recommended while breastfeeding, as hormones may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about safe alternatives. Teenagers: This medicine can be used safely in teenagers who have already had their first period. Older adults (over 35): Women over 35 who smoke should NOT use this medicine due to a significantly higher risk of serious cardiovascular events including heart attack and stroke. Women with certain health conditions — including a history of blood clots, stroke, heart attack, certain types of migraines (with aura), liver disease, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or certain hormone-sensitive cancers — should not use this medicine. Always tell your doctor your full medical history before starting this pill.
